questions.q: What is the strict requirement of Continuous Integration that's easy to overlook?
options: Every developer must work on the same branch with no branching allowed
The main branch must stay in a releasable state at all times, with broken builds fixed as top priority
Tests only need to run once a week
CI requires deploying to production on every merge
questions.explain: CI requires more than just frequent merging — the main branch must stay releasable at all times. A red build on main should be the team's top priority to fix.

questions.q: What distinguishes Continuous Delivery from Continuous Deployment?
options: They are identical practices with different names
Continuous Delivery keeps a human approval step before production; Continuous Deployment removes it entirely
Continuous Deployment never runs automated tests
Continuous Delivery only applies to staging environments
questions.explain: Continuous Delivery means every passing build is release-ready, but a human still decides when to deploy. Continuous Deployment removes that last manual gate — passing changes deploy to production automatically.

questions.q: Why might Northbridge Retail choose NOT to use Continuous Deployment straight to production?
options: Because automated tests are impossible to write
Because business reasons, like avoiding a release right before Black Friday, may call for a human-controlled release timing
Because Continuous Deployment is illegal
Because Kubernetes doesn't support automatic deployments
questions.explain: Even when code is fully tested and ready, a business may want to control exactly when a release reaches customers — which is what Continuous Delivery's human-approved gate provides.

questions.q: In the comparison table, which practice is described as NOT guaranteeing a build is always release-ready?
options: Continuous Integration
Continuous Delivery
Continuous Deployment
All three guarantee it equally
questions.explain: CI guarantees frequent automated build and test, but does not by itself guarantee every build is packaged and ready to release — that's what Continuous Delivery adds.

questions.q: A common real-world pattern mentioned in the lesson is to deploy automatically to staging but require approval for production. Which combination of practices does this describe?
options: Continuous Integration only, with no delivery or deployment
Continuous Deployment to staging, Continuous Delivery (human-approved) to production
Continuous Deployment to both staging and production
No CI/CD practice describes this pattern
questions.explain: This mixed pattern is common in practice: fast, automatic deployment to lower-risk environments like staging, combined with a human-approved gate for production releases.
